chapter: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
title: Sound-track calls from Forbstein and Georgie Stoll; first black contractor
summary: Warner and MGM music directors called him after Sebastian's; Stoll made him a contractor for a Louis Armstrong street scene.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: So, what -- you started, as soon as there were sound tracks to be played, you were in there playing those?

Yeah, I started with the sound track playings. I used to get a whole lot of calls from out at Warner Brothers, First National, from Leo Forbstein (PHONETIC), who was the musical director out there. He used to come and hear me at Sebastian's Cotton Club and he cut a liking to me and thought I had a little bit of talent. So, when he wanted something special played, he used to call me. Then, one of the directors out at Warner -- at MGM, he was an ex-violin player, by the name of Georgie Stole (PHONETIC) and when he became music director out there, he used to be one of the people that would come into Sebastian's Cotton Club in the old days. As a matter of fact, I can remember him very clearly, driving up into

the parking lot with his brand new Dusenbery convertible and he now lives up around the Morrell Castle (PHONETIC), up North here. As a matter of fact, he's the owner of part of the old Morrell Castle.

Georgie Stole, he was the first guy that ever gave a black guy a chance to be a contractor for a musical scene in pictures in Hollywood and that happened to be me at the time. It was at one of the freelance studios and it featured Louis Armstrong in a street scene, a walking scene, in 1937, '38 period. I contracted the band, which was a walking band, 45 pieces, and we made the recordings and everything for it. I can thank him for being so nice. That was Georgie Stole.
Do you remember the name of the picture?
Can't remember the picture, but it was made with Louis Armstrong around 1937, '38. We had a walking band in the street. I got all the fellows together.
Do you remember who all you hired?
Oh, I had a whole lot of guys -- Red Callender, Lee Young, Oscar Bradley, Eddie Barefield (PHONETIC), Ernie Royal -- just a whole gang, whoever was the better guys around the place, they were there.
Oh, I can't remember no more. That's a long time from '37 to '77 is 40 years, isn't it?
